### Observed differences

- Work on A01, A03, A13, A14 and A17 was reallocated between resources. In the earlier window, each of these activities was spread thinly over many resources — no single resource handled more than about 9 in 100 executions, and roughly 46 in 100 went to a long tail of occasional resources. In the later window, a largely different set of resources appears: one previously prominent resource (User_10, about 8–9 in 100 on each of these activities before) is no longer observed on any of them, while new resources take shares of similar size (the largest, User_41, about 7–8 in 100). Profile dissimilarity is about 0.21–0.32 on a 0–1 scale, each profile rests on roughly 200–330 observations per window, and every difference exceeds all but about 1 in 2000 random re-splits. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]

- A11 moved from shared to single-resource handling: in the earlier window about ten different resources executed it (largest share about 15 in 100), while in the later window every observed A11 execution was assigned to one resource, User_31 (100 in 100, maximal dissimilarity of 1.0), based on 113 vs 104 observations. [ASSIGN003]

- Elapsed time between consecutive completions shortened for A04→A01: the median gap fell from about 25 hours to about 13 hours (mean from about 43 to about 15 hours; three-quarters of gaps within about 46 hours before vs about 19 hours after), with 200 observed pairs in each window. [TWAIT001]

- For A09→A23, the typical gap fell from about 9 hours to about half an hour (mean about 13 to about 3 hours), and the number of observed consecutive pairs dropped from 40 to 25. [TWAIT002]

- No structural difference reached the screening thresholds: 0 control-flow items qualified, where about 0.17 would be expected by chance in a stable process. [screening]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports the possibility that resource allocation changed. On A01, A03, A13, A14, A17, execution shifted from one group of resources that handled these activities earlier and largely stopped appearing afterwards (including User_10 at about 8–9 in 100 each) to a largely different group that took over similar shares (including User_41 at about 7–8 in 100); in addition, A11 changed from being shared across about ten resources to being executed only by User_31. This rests on six qualifying assignment indicators where the resource family expected about 0.004 by chance, on the same incoming and outgoing resource groups recurring across all five swap activities, and on every difference being larger than in all but about 1 in 2000 random re-splits. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]

Limitations: A13 and A14 show identical profiles, so those two items likely describe the same underlying behaviour rather than independent confirmations; the evidence cannot show whether the five activity-level swaps and the A11 concentration stem from one coordinated reassignment or from separate per-activity changes, and it cannot say why allocation changed. [ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005]

Other differences: A consistent timing change accompanies the reallocation: gaps between consecutive completions shortened for A04→A01 (median about 25 to about 13 hours, 200 pairs per window) and for A09→A23 (median about 9 hours to about half an hour, 40 vs 25 pairs); the time family produced 2 qualifying items against about 0.016 expected by chance. The evidence cannot show whether this is an independent change in timing or a side effect of the reallocation, and the A09→A23 estimate rests on only 25 observations in the later window. [TWAIT001, TWAIT002]

No change to structure or ordering is indicated at these thresholds, since no control-flow item qualified (0 against about 0.17 expected by chance). [screening]
